stem: What is **depreciation**?

options.content: The part of an asset's cost used up in a period
options.rationale: Correct: it allocates the cost over the asset's useful life.

options.content: Cash put aside each year to buy a replacement asset later
options.rationale: No cash is set aside; depreciation is a non-cash expense.

options.content: The amount received when a non-current asset is sold
options.rationale: That is the sale proceeds (disposal value).

options.content: The fall in the market price of goods held for resale
options.rationale: Goods for resale are inventory, not non-current assets.

explanation: Depreciation charges part of a non-current asset's cost as an expense in each period that benefits from the asset.

stem: A business replaces its computers because new models are much faster, although the old ones still work. Which cause of depreciation is this?

options.rationale: Correct: the asset is out of date, not worn out.
The computers still work; they have not worn out.
Depletion applies to natural resources such as mines and quarries.
That applies to assets with a fixed legal life, such as a lease.

explanation: Obsolescence is loss of value because better or more efficient assets have become available.

stem: Which accounting concept is the main reason for charging depreciation?

options.rationale: Correct: the cost is matched against the income the asset helps to earn over its life.
Going concern supports valuing assets at cost, but it is not the reason for spreading the cost.
That separates the owner from the business.
Duality explains double entry, not why cost is spread over years.

explanation: Depreciation spreads the cost of a non-current asset over the periods that benefit, applying the matching concept.

stem: Which non-current asset is most suitably depreciated by the **revaluation** method?

options.rationale: Vehicles lose most value early: reducing balance suits them.
A lease loses value evenly with time: straight line suits it.

options.content: Loose tools in a motor repair workshop
options.rationale: Correct: many small items, impractical to depreciate one by one.

options.content: Office furniture bought on one date
options.rationale: A single purchase used evenly suits straight line.

explanation: The revaluation method values groups of small items (loose tools, crockery, livestock) at each year end.

stem: A machine costing US\$15,000 is depreciated at 20% per annum on the reducing-balance method. What is the depreciation charge for the **second** year?

options.rationale: This is 20% of cost: the straight-line answer.
This is the net book value at the end of year 2.
Correct: 20% of the net book value of 12,000 at the start of year 2.
This is the accumulated depreciation after two years at 20% of cost.

stem: Why is the reducing-balance method often chosen for motor vehicles?

options.content: It reduces the total depreciation charged over the vehicle's life
options.rationale: Over the whole life the total charged is about the same; only the timing differs.

options.content: Vehicles lose most of their value in the early years of use
options.rationale: Correct: the high early charges match the fast early fall in value.

options.content: The charge is the same every year, so it is easy to compare
options.rationale: That describes straight line.

options.content: It ignores the residual value of the vehicle
options.rationale: Ignoring residual value is not a reason to choose a method.

explanation: Vehicles lose value fastest when new, and their repair costs rise as they age, so falling depreciation charges keep the total yearly cost more even.
hints: Think about how a vehicle's market value falls after it is bought.

stem: A business buys a machine on 1 October 2025. Its policy is to charge 12% per annum on cost, time apportioned. The year end is 31 December. For how many months is depreciation charged in 2025?

options.rationale: This counts the months before the purchase.
Correct: October, November and December.
This would be the policy of a full year in the year of purchase.
This would be the policy of no depreciation in the year of purchase.

explanation: Time apportioned means only the months the asset was owned: 1 October to 31 December is 3 months.
hints: Count the months from the purchase date to the year end.

stem: Tatenda buys a hammer mill for US\$32,000. He expects to use it for five years and then sell it for US\$4,000. What is its net book value after **three** years using the straight-line method?

options.rationale: This ignores the residual value (32,000 ÷ 5 = 6,400 a year).
This is the accumulated depreciation, not the net book value.
This is the value after two years.

stem: Charging depreciation reduces the cash balance of the business.
explanation: False. Depreciation is a non-cash expense; cash left the business when the asset was bought.

stem: Under the reducing-balance method the depreciation charge falls every year.
explanation: True. The same percentage is applied to a smaller net book value each year.

stem: Match each asset with the cause of depreciation that mainly affects it.

left.content: A minibus used daily on rough roads
A 15-year lease on a shop in Gweru
Mobile phones used by sales staff

explanation: Physical use wears out vehicles; mines are used up; leases expire with time; technology goes out of date.

stem: Complete the formulas.

payload.template: Straight line: (cost − {{blank:a}}) ÷ useful life. Reducing balance: rate × {{blank:b}} at the start of the year. Revaluation: opening value + purchases − {{blank:c}}.

explanation: These three formulas cover every depreciation calculation at this level.

stem: Chipo runs a restaurant in Masvingo. Her crockery and cutlery were valued at US\$3,150 on 1 January 2025. During the year she bought more for US\$1,240 and sold some old items for US\$180 cash. On 31 December 2025 the crockery and cutlery were valued at US\$3,420. Calculate the depreciation for the year.
explanation: 3,150 + 1,240 − 180 − 3,420 = 790. Forgetting to deduct the 180 received gives 970.
workedSolution: 1. 3,150 + 1,240 − 180 − 3,420 = 790. Forgetting to deduct the 180 received gives 970.
hints: Opening value + purchases − sale proceeds − closing value.

stem: Sipho bought a generator on 1 June 2025 for US\$14,400. He depreciates generators at 15% per annum on cost, on a monthly basis. His year end is 31 December. Calculate the depreciation charge for 2025.
explanation: Annual charge 15% × 14,400 = 2,160. June to December = 7 months: 2,160 × 7/12 = 1,260. A full year would be 2,160; counting only 5 months gives 900.
workedSolution: 1. Annual charge 15% × 14,400 = 2,160. June to December = 7 months: 2,160 × 7/12 = 1,260. A full year would be 2,160; counting only 5 months gives 900.
hints: June to December inclusive is how many months?

stem: Nyasha bought a tractor for her farm near Chinhoyi on 1 January 2023 for US\$40,000. She depreciates it at 30% per annum using the reducing-balance method. Calculate the net book value of the tractor at 31 December 2025.
hints: Work year by year: each charge is 30% of the previous closing net book value.

stem: A printer for a school club costs US\$7,650, has a useful life of 6 years and a residual value of US\$450. Calculate the annual straight-line depreciation.
explanation: (7,650 − 450) ÷ 6 = 1,200. Ignoring the residual value gives 1,275.

stem: State **two** causes of depreciation and give an example of an asset affected by each.

points.description: One cause with a suitable asset, e.g. wear and tear: delivery van
A second cause with a suitable asset, e.g. obsolescence: computer; passage of time: lease; depletion: quarry

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Wear and tear, for example a delivery van used every day; obsolescence, for example a computer replaced by a faster model.

explanation: Any two of wear and tear, obsolescence, passage of time and depletion, each with a matching asset.

stem: Farai says he will not charge depreciation this year because profits are low and 'the machine has not cost any money this year'. Explain why he is wrong.

points.description: The machine has been used to earn this year's income, so part of its cost must be matched against it (matching concept)
Without depreciation profit would be overstated
and the machine would be overstated in the statement of financial position / the method should be applied consistently every year

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Depreciation is not a payment but an allocation of cost. The machine helped earn this year's income, so part of its cost is an expense of this year (matching). Leaving it out overstates profit and the asset's value, and breaks the consistency concept.

explanation: Depreciation must be charged every year the asset is used, whatever the level of profit.

stem:
Thandeka runs a courier service in Harare. On 1 January 2023 she bought a motorcycle fleet for US\$27,000. She expects to use it for four years and then sell it for US\$3,000. She is comparing two depreciation methods:

- Method 1: straight line.
- Method 2: reducing balance at 40% per annum.

Her year end is 31 December.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the annual depreciation charge using Method 1.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the depreciation charge for 2023 using Method 2.
parts.explanation: 40% × 27,000 = 10,800 (the residual value is not deducted under reducing balance).
parts.workedSolution: 1. 40% × 27,000 = 10,800 (the residual value is not deducted under reducing balance).

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the depreciation charge for 2024 using Method 2.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the net book value at 31 December 2025 using Method 2.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: By how much is the total depreciation charged for 2023–2025 under Method 2 greater than under Method 1?

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Advise Thandeka which method to use. Give a reason.

points.description: Motorcycles lose most value in the early years / repairs rise later so the total yearly cost is more even

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Method 2, reducing balance: motorcycles lose value fastest when new, and as repair costs rise the depreciation falls, keeping the yearly cost of using them more even. (Straight line accepted only with a reason such as simplicity.)

parts.explanation: Name the method and link the reason to how the asset loses value.

explanation:
Schedule under Method 2:

| Year | Depreciation US\$ | Accumulated depreciation US\$ | Net book value US\$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2023 | 10,800 | 10,800 | 16,200 |
| 2024 | 6,480 | 17,280 | 9,720 |
| 2025 | 3,888 | 21,168 | 5,832 |
hints: Reducing balance ignores residual value: apply the rate to the net book value.
Each method's total over three years is the sum of the three charges.

stem:
Tendai owns a panel-beating workshop in Gweru. His year end is 31 December.

| Information | US\$ |
| --- | ---: |
| Loose tools at valuation, 1 January 2025 | 4,860 |
| Loose tools bought during 2025 | 1,575 |
| Loose tools at valuation, 31 December 2025 | 5,120 |
| Spray-painting equipment bought 1 January 2024, at cost | 12,600 |

The spray-painting equipment has a useful life of five years and a residual value of US\$600. It is depreciated by the straight-line method.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the depreciation of loose tools for 2025.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the annual depreciation of the spray-painting equipment.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the net book value of the equipment at 31 December 2025.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Why is the revaluation method used for the loose tools?

options.content: Loose tools never wear out or lose value through use
options.rationale: They do wear out and get lost; that is why their value falls.

options.content: The revaluation method always gives a lower charge
options.rationale: The charge depends on the valuations, not the method.

options.content: Tools bought during the year must not be depreciated at all
options.rationale: Purchases are included in the calculation.

options.content: There are too many small items to depreciate one by one
options.rationale: Correct.

parts.explanation: Loose tools are numerous, cheap and easily lost, so a year-end valuation is used.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: State **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of the revaluation method.

points.description: Advantage: simple for many small items / reflects actual loss, including losses and breakages
Disadvantage: valuation is subjective / depends on judgement, so profit may vary

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: It is simple and reflects real losses of small items; but valuations depend on judgement, so the charge can be inconsistent.

explanation: This item practises the revaluation and straight-line methods.
hints: Revaluation: opening value + purchases − closing value.

stem: Which statement about the **straight-line** method is correct?

options.content: The charge is highest in the first year
options.rationale: That describes reducing balance.

options.content: The asset is valued at each year end to find the charge
options.rationale: That describes revaluation.

options.content: The residual value is depreciated as well
options.rationale: Only cost less residual value is spread over the life.

options.content: The same amount is charged in each year of the asset's useful life
options.rationale: Correct.

explanation: Straight line spreads (cost − residual value) equally over the useful life.
